title: Feds were already looking to revive P3 funding for American Legion Bridge before Moore meeting
summary: Even before this month's meeting between Gov. Wes Moore and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy jump-started talk of public-private funding to replace the American Legion Bridge, federal officials were already moving in that direction.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters January 25, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters January 25, 2026

Even before this month’s meeting between Gov. Wes Moore and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy jump-started talk of public-private funding to replace the American Legion Bridge, federal officials were already moving in that direction.

In a Federal Register post Dec. 11, the Federal Highway Administration solicited “public input and proposals on innovative project delivery methods to ensure cost-effective and efficient reconstruction of the American Legion Memorial Bridge.” The post noted that the state cannot fund the project on its own, before noting that a public-private partnership (P3) could do the trick.

Just over a month later, Moore and Duffy announced they had agreed on “the need to speed up the reconstruction and leverage innovative approaches like a public private partnership (P3) that will ensure Maryland, Virginia, and D.C. commuters can soon experience some much needed traffic relief from the most congested corridor in America.”

It was a change of course for Moore who inherited the framework of a P3 deal from his predecessor, Gov. Larry Hogan (R), for the American Legion Bridge and additional toll lanes on the Capital Beltway. But the state and Transurban, the company behind the proposed P3, were not able to finalize the deal, and P3 funding fell by the wayside.

In a meeting with reporters Jan. 16, Moore said he was never “against P3s. I’m against dumb P3s.”

“And I think we had dumb P3s that were put in place before,” Moore said. “I’m for P3s. Yes, there is going to be private-sector involvement, but the entire upside can’t be on the private sector while the public sector gets hooked.

State reopens door to private funding for American Legion Bridge reconstruction

“And so, we’re just going to make sure that we’re thinking smartly about ways we’re going to apply the P3 into this. But I do think that P3s are necessary and required for a lot of the major projects that we want to get done in Maryland,” he said.

The meeting with Duffy also touched on replacement of the Francis Scott Key Bridge.

In the days after the bridge was struck by a loaded container ship and collapsed into the Patapsco River in March 2024, then-President Joe Biden pledged that the federal government would fund 100% of its replacement. Congress put that pledge into law in late 2024, a legal promise that Maryland lawmakers have repeatedly cited when President Donald Trump makes threats about federal funding for the project.

But in the days after the collapse, state officials also said it would cost just under $2 billion for the bridge replacement, which could be done as early as 2028. The latest estimates say the project could cost up to $5.2 billion and take until 2030, opening the door to new criticism from the Trump administration.

Duffy and Trump have also been critical of the use of contractors based on race or sex. Moore this month dismissed those complaints, saying increases in the estimated cost of the bridge replacement had nothing to do with choice of contractors and everything to do with required changes to the bridge design for safety reason, additional materials to go with those changes and higher costs of those materials as a result of tariffs and inflation.

State officials have long said that they will put any money they win in lawsuits against the owners of the Dali, the ship that struck the bridge, toward the bottom line on the project. In the joint statement after their meeting, Moore and Duffy said they “made significant progress on cost sharing … to ensure fairness” on the Key Bridge.

But that wording left some, like Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) confused.

Ferguson called the joint announcement “very promising” and said he was “looking forward to hearing the details” of the meeting. But he seemed surprised when asked about the possibility of “cost sharing” mentioned in the Moore-Duffy statement.

“I have to look more into that,” Ferguson said. “My understanding is that cost sharing is not a component of it. It’s 100% covered. So, I have to get back to you on that.”

“The good news is that the repaying, or the payment for the rebuild of the Francis Scott Key Bridge is in federal law. It’s in statute,” Ferguson said. “It is not through executive order or regulation that can be waived by the stroke of a pen and would require an act of Congress to restrict that funding.

“Should we be wary? I think we have to be. I think every assumption of what we thought or we could assume about the relationship between the state and the federal government is now up for question.”

Moore did not elaborate on the discussions regarding federal funding for the Key Bridge replacement.

“I think our teams are working very closely, and we are ensuring that in this time, we are going to be able to do something that’s not just going to make the people of the state of Maryland proud, but we’re going to do something to make the people this country proud,” Moore told reporters a day after meeting with Duffy.

It’s also not clear how the American Legion Bridge Project will progress. It is also unclear what role, if any, the Virginia Department of Transportation will have in a new American Legion Bridge.

Moore, in statements following the meeting with Duffy, described the American Legion Bridge project as “stalled.”

“We want to get this done quickly. And the thing that we both acknowledge is that when I first came on board, what we inherited were just stalled projects. Right?” Moore said. “The Purple Line was a stalled project, the ALB [American Legion Bridge] was a stalled project. And I told the secretary, and I think, you know, he agreed, we’re going to work together, because I refuse to hand off stalled projects to my successors.”

Doug Mayer, a spokesperson for Hogan, rejected Moore’s characterization of the American Legion Bridge project as stalled when he came into office. Mayer said Moore is “not misrepresenting the truth. He’s lying.”

Hogan had announced a plan to widen the bridge along with Maryland sections of Interstate 495 before Moore took office under a P3 agreement with a consortium led by Australia-based Transurban. The Transurban-led consortium was to expand the bridge and highway using managed toll lanes.

Mayer said the Hogan administration left the project “on the 99-yard line.”

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

“He inherited a project that the former administration had spent years fighting for and had finally gotten to a place where all it needed was to go in front of the Board of Public Works,” Mayer said. “He (Moore) said he was going to pause it and get more feedback and for silly things like equity and the rest of that nonsense. What’s been going on for the last three years?”

Critics at the time complained that the proposal would benefit wealthy motorists and harm the environment. The project was similar to one Transurban constructed in Virginia.

Moore, responding to a question from a reporter, called the project a shared interest of both states and one that both states should share responsibility.

“I think for a lot of things that were done before, there was not a mutually shared both interest, ambition or incentive to be able to get the work done,” Moore said. “I will be working very closely with our friends in the Commonwealth of Virginia to make sure that the p3 that is done, that Maryland actually has a proper seat at the table when we’re looking at what those proper and those final dynamics look like.”
